notes:
Here are the verse-by-verse notes for Luke 7:1–25, drawn from the sources available through the approved sites.

---

## The Centurion's Servant (vv. 1–10)

**v. 1: "When Jesus had concluded His discourse in the hearing of the people, He went to Capernaum."**

The "discourse" refers to the Sermon on the Plain (Luke 6:20–49), which the Pulpit Commentary calls "the great manifesto of the new Master." Capernaum was Jesus' adopted home city during his public ministry—his headquarters from which he went out on missionary tours and to which he returned. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/luke/7.htm) Enduring Word likewise notes that after the sermon, Jesus came to "his city of residence" (Matthew 4:13). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-7/)

**v. 2: "There a highly valued servant of a centurion was sick and about to die."**

The Pulpit Commentary points out that the Greek word is literally "slave," not a hired servant, which makes the centurion's tender concern extraordinary for a culture where masters had the legal right to kill sick or injured slaves. The centurion was a Roman officer commanding roughly a hundred soldiers. Matthew's parallel account identifies the illness as paralysis accompanied by severe pain, and the Pulpit suggests "some dangerous form of rheumatic fever" that attacks the heart. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/luke/7.htm) Gill notes the servant "was dear unto him" and compares this to the rabbinic account of Gamaliel's beloved servant Tabi. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/luke-7.html)

**v. 3: "When the centurion heard about Jesus, he sent some Jewish elders to ask Him to come and heal his servant."**

The centurion did not go himself. The Pulpit Commentary explains he probably "had made up his mind that this Jesus was no mortal man" and therefore felt unworthy to approach him directly. The elders he sent were "some of the official elders connected with his own synagogue," men who could more gracefully plead his cause. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/luke/7.htm) Enduring Word adds that the centurion likely "did not think himself worthy of a personal meeting with Jesus" and perhaps assumed Jesus would not want to meet a Gentile. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-7/)

**v. 4: "They came to Jesus and pleaded with Him earnestly, 'This man is worthy to have You grant this…'"**

Gill's Exposition observes that the elders' speech "savours of their pharisaic tenet and notion of merit, and is very different from the sense the poor centurion had of himself." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/luke-7.html) Enduring Word draws the contrast: "The elders said he was worthy; he said he was not worthy. They praised him for building a house of worship; he felt unworthy that Jesus would come to his house." This sets up the lesson that "we can come to Jesus directly… even when we are unworthy; He justifies the ungodly (Romans 4:5)." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-7/)

**v. 5: "for he loves our nation and has built our synagogue."**

The Pulpit Commentary elaborates that this centurion was likely a "proselyte of the gate"—a Gentile who had accepted the faith of Israel without submitting to circumcision or burdensome ceremonial rites incompatible with his military profession. Every mention of centurions in the Gospels and Acts is favourable (Cornelius in Acts 10, the centurion at the cross, the centurion who conveyed Paul to Rome). Modern travellers report that among the ruins of Capernaum are the remains of a white marble synagogue from the Herodian period—possibly this soldier's noble gift. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/luke/7.htm)

**v. 6: "So Jesus went with them. But when He was not far from the house, the centurion sent friends with the message: 'Lord, do not trouble Yourself, for I am not worthy to have You come under my roof.'"**

Augustine's comment on this verse, preserved in the Pulpit Commentary: "By saying that he was unworthy, he showed himself worthy of Christ's entering, not within his walls, but within his heart." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/luke/7.htm) Enduring Word quotes Spurgeon: "Two features of character blend in him which do not often meet in such graceful harmony. He won the high opinion of others and yet he held a low estimation of himself." Spurgeon adds: "Your faith will not murder your humility, your humility will not stab at your faith; but the two will go hand in hand to heaven like a brave brother and a fair sister." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-7/)

From a Reformed perspective, R.C. Sproul (Ligonier) says: "The centurion understood grace. He understood it in a way that few people in Israel understood it… 'You don't have to come. Just say the word.' That is remarkable." (https://learn.ligonier.org/sermons/centurions-servant)

**v. 7: "That is why I did not consider myself worthy to come to You. But just say the word, and my servant will be healed."**

The Pulpit Commentary notes that the centurion's faith had "risen above the need of an outward sign, such as a touch or even the sound of a living voice. He needed no contact with the fringe of the Master's garment… The word the Master would speak would be enough." It then makes a theological point: Christ commends this, whereas Martha (John 11:22) was reproved for saying "I know whatsoever thou shalt ask of God he will give it thee"—teaching that Christ "is the Source of blessings, which he could not be unless he were God." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/luke/7.htm) John Calvin, quoted at Ligonier, states: "he who, by the mere expression of his will, restores health to men, must possess supreme authority." (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/faith-centurion)

**v. 8: "For I myself am a man under authority, with soldiers under me. I tell one to go, and he goes…"**

The Pulpit Commentary reads between the lines: the centurion's reasoning is, "If I, who am under many a superior—the chiliarch of my thousand, the tribunes of my legion, my emperor who commands at Rome—yet receive a ready and willing obedience… how much more thou, who hast no one above thee, no superior, when thou commandest disease, one of thy ministers, will it not at once obey?" It adds that the centurion inferred that Jesus had at his command thousands of the "heavenly army" (cf. Luke 2:13; Matthew 26:53). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/luke/7.htm) Desiring God observes: "He knew Jesus had authority from the Father to command the natural world. He knew proximity was no factor. Jesus could speak disease out of existence from any distance." (https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/the-centurion-faith-that-made-jesus-marvel)

**v. 9: "When Jesus heard this, He marveled at the centurion. Turning to the crowd following Him, He said, 'I tell you, not even in Israel have I found such great faith.'"**

Jesus only "marvelled" (Greek *thaumazo*) twice in the Gospels: here at great faith, and in Mark 6:6 at the unbelief of his own townspeople in Nazareth. (https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/the-centurion-faith-that-made-jesus-marvel) Augustine, cited in the Pulpit Commentary, asks: "Who had inspired that faith but he who now admires it?" He adds that Christ admires "for our good, that we may imitate the centurion's faith." Augustine also remarks that "the Lord had found in the oleaster [wild olive] what he had not found in the olive." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/luke/7.htm)

Desiring God calls this "a gospel irony"—the only person whose faith made Jesus marvel was a Roman soldier, a Gentile "stranger to the covenant," stationed in Palestine to keep the Jews under pagan rule. "He was a first fruit and foreshadow of what Jesus had come to bring about: that 'many would come from the east and west and recline at table with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven' (Matthew 8:11)." (https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/faith-that-made-jesus-marvel)

**v. 10: "And when the messengers returned to the house, they found the servant in good health."**

The Pulpit Commentary notes Farrar's suggestion that "convalescent" is a more accurate rendering than "whole," and that the Greek term is one of the distinctive medical words found in Luke's Gospel. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/luke/7.htm) Enduring Word concludes: Jesus "both answered the centurion's unselfish request and proved that He really did have the authority the centurion trusted Him to have." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-7/)

## The Widow of Nain (vv. 11–17)

**v. 11: "Soon afterward, Jesus went to a town called Nain. His disciples went with Him, accompanied by a large crowd."**

Nain (Hebrew *na'im*, "lovely") is located on the north-west slope of Jebel el Duhy (Little Hermon), near Endor, about twenty-five miles from Capernaum. Today it is a squalid village still called Nein. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/luke/7.htm) Luke alone records this miracle. The Pulpit Commentary speculates that the "devout women" of Luke 8:1–3 preserved the memory of this event and passed it on to Luke. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/luke/7.htm)

**v. 12: "As He approached the town gate, He saw a dead man being carried out, the only son of his mother, and she was a widow. And a large crowd from the town was with her."**

Jews buried their dead outside the city because corpses were ceremonially unclean, and funerals typically occurred on the day of death. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/luke/7.htm) Gill explains the Jewish burial customs in detail: a child under a month was carried in the bosom; a full month old in a small coffin in the arms; a year old in a coffin on the shoulder; three years and upward on a bier or bed. The large crowd attending indicates the young man was well known and respected. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/luke-7.html)

**v. 13: "When the Lord saw her, He had compassion on her and said, 'Do not weep.'"**

The Pulpit Commentary observes that the title "the Lord" (Greek *kyrios*) used by itself is rare in the Gospels—"Jesus" being the usual term. This reflects Luke's post-resurrection perspective: neither Luke nor Paul had been with Jesus during His earthly ministry, and they always looked on him as "the Lord risen from the dead, enthroned in heaven." Significantly, Jesus worked this miracle "not from a distinct purpose to offer credentials of his mission, but proceeded rather from his intense compassion." No one asked Him; He acted purely from divine pity. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/luke/7.htm) Gill likewise notes that Jesus "helped her without being asked to do it, as usual in other cases." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/luke-7.html)

**v. 14: "Then He went up and touched the coffin, and those carrying it stood still. 'Young man,' He said, 'I tell you, get up!'"**

The "coffin" (the BSB rendering) was actually an open bier on which the corpse lay wrapped in linen—not the enclosed box we think of today. Touching a bier was considered polluting. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/luke/7.htm) The People's New Testament says: "There was an authority in not only the words but the acts of the Lord which compelled obedience." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pnt/luke/7.htm)

John Calvin comments: "By touching the coffin he intended perhaps to show, that he would by no means shrink from death and the grave, in order to obtain life for us. He not only deigns to touch us with his hand, in order to quicken us when we are dead, but, in order that he might raise us to heaven, himself descends into the grave." (https://biblehub.com/library/calvin/commentary_on_matthew_mark_luke_volume_1/luke_7_11-17.htm)

The Pulpit Commentary contrasts Jesus with the Old Testament prophets: "Elijah mourned long over the son of the widow of Sarepta, Elisha repeatedly stretched himself as he agonized in prayer upon the lifeless corpse of the Shunammite boy, Peter prayed very earnestly over the body of Dorcas at Lydda. The Master, with one solitary word, brings the spirit from its mysterious habitation back to its old earthly tenement." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/luke/7.htm)

**v. 15: "And the dead man sat up and began to speak! Then Jesus gave him back to his mother."**

Jamieson-Fausset-Brown exclaims: "What mingled majesty and grace shines in this scene! The Resurrection and the Life in human flesh, with a word of command, bringing back life to the dead body; Incarnate Compassion summoning its absolute power to dry a widow's tears!" (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/luke/7.htm) Enduring Word clarifies: "This young man was not resurrected but resuscitated; he rose from the dead only to die again. God promises that we will be resurrected and rise from the dead never to die again." It also recounts the famous Moody anecdote: D.L. Moody searched the Gospels for a funeral sermon by Jesus and found none, "because every funeral Jesus attended He broke up by raising the dead!" (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-7/)

**v. 16: "A sense of awe swept over all of them, and they glorified God. 'A great prophet has appeared among us!' they said. 'God has visited His people!'"**

Calvin distinguishes the fear here as a good fear: "Unbelievers either tremble and are dismayed; or, struck with alarm, murmur against God: while devout and godly persons, moved by reverence, willingly humble themselves." The people rendered "not only homage, but thanksgiving." (https://biblehub.com/library/calvin/commentary_on_matthew_mark_luke_volume_1/luke_7_11-17.htm) The Pulpit Commentary notes that after four centuries since Malachi, the people recognized that at last God again had visited his people—though they saw Jesus only as "a great Prophet," not yet as the Divine Messiah. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/luke/7.htm)

**v. 17: "And the news about Jesus spread throughout Judea and all the surrounding region."**

The report of this miracle—raising a dead man already on his way to burial—spread widely and contributed to the growing fame of Jesus. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/luke-7.html)

## John the Baptist's Question (vv. 18–25)

**v. 18: "Then John's disciples informed him about all these things."**

John was in prison (imprisoned by Herod Antipas, see Luke 3:19–20), but his disciples had free access to him. Gill notes that John's disciples reported these miracles "not as commending Christ for them; but as envying, grieving, and complaining, that he carried away all the honour and glory from John their master, for whom they had the greatest regard." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/luke-7.html) Enduring Word notes that some of Jesus' own disciples had started as John's disciples (e.g., Andrew, John 1:35–40), and it was noted when Jesus' disciples began to outnumber John's (John 4:1). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-7/)

**v. 19: "So John called two of his disciples and sent them to ask the Lord, 'Are You the One who was to come, or should we look for someone else?'"**

This verse has divided interpreters historically. The Pulpit Commentary outlines the two views:

- **View A (majority of modern expositors, including Meyer, Godet, Farrar):** John's own faith wavered. His long, hopeless imprisonment and Jesus' failure to launch a political deliverance caused genuine doubt. The Pulpit Commentary favours this view, noting that Scripture "while it tenderly and lovingly handles the characters of its heroes, it never flinches from the truth."

- **View B (many early Church Fathers—Jerome, Ambrose, Chrysostom, and later Calvin, Beza, Melancthon):** John did not doubt at all; he sent his disciples for *their* sake, so that they might see Jesus' works and believe. Jerome wrote: "John does not put this question from ignorance, for he himself had proclaimed Christ to be 'the Lamb of God.' But… John, now about to be slain by Herod, sends his disciples to Jesus, in order that, by this occasion, they who were jealous of the fame of Jesus might see his mighty works and believe in him."

(https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/luke/7.htm)

Gill firmly holds View B: "not that he doubted that Jesus was the Messiah; nor was it for his own satisfaction so much that he sent these disciples of his with this question, but for theirs; and to remove all doubt and hesitation from them about Christ." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/luke-7.html)

Enduring Word holds View A, suggesting John "perhaps… had himself misunderstood the ministry of the Messiah" and "thought that if Jesus were really the Messiah, He would perform works connected with a political deliverance of Israel—or at least the deliverance of John, who was in prison." It quotes Geldenhuys: "John was already in prison, and things began to appear incomprehensible to him. He had expected that Christ would speedily destroy the powers of darkness and judge the unrighteous. But instead of doing this, He leaves him, His forerunner, helpless in prison." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-7/)

**v. 20: "When the men came to Jesus, they said, 'John the Baptist sent us to ask, "Are You the One who was to come, or should we look for someone else?"'"**

This repeats the question from v. 19. Neither commentary adds substantial new material here beyond noting the messengers' arrival. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/luke-7.html)

**v. 21: "At that very hour Jesus healed many people of their diseases, afflictions, and evil spirits, and He gave sight to many who were blind."**

Cyril of Alexandria (quoted in the Pulpit Commentary) explains the timing: "He knew as God what John's design was in sending to him, and he put it into his heart to send at that very time when he himself was working many miracles which were the true answer to the question." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/luke/7.htm) Gill notes that Jesus cured "many of their infirmities; bodily weaknesses and disorders: and plagues; which were inflicted on them as scourges and corrections for sin, very severe diseases, as epilepsies, leprosies, palsies." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/luke-7.html)

**v. 22: "So He replied, 'Go back and report to John what you have seen and heard: The blind receive sight, the lame walk, the lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead are raised, and the good news is preached to the poor.'"**

Jesus does not give a direct "yes" or "no." Instead He points to fulfilment of Messianic prophecy. Enduring Word maps each item to Isaiah:

- The blind see → Isaiah 61:1, 35:5
- The lame walk → Isaiah 35:6
- The deaf hear → Isaiah 35:5
- The dead live → Isaiah 26:19
- The poor hear good news → Isaiah 61:1

(https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-7/)

Gill emphasises that opening the eyes of the blind, especially those born blind, "was what was never heard of before, from the beginning of the world; and which, as it is an instance of Christ's almighty power, showing him to be God; so it was a fulfilment of a prophecy concerning him as the Messiah." On "the dead are raised," Gill says: "this is what none but the mighty God can do." On the gospel preached to the poor, he notes this was prophesied in Isaiah 61:1. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/luke-7.html)

Enduring Word adds that Jesus "wanted to assure both John and his disciples that He was the Messiah. But He also reminded them that His power would be displayed mostly in humble acts of service, meeting individual needs and not in spectacular displays of political deliverance." It quotes G. Campbell Morgan: "For the most part, the way of the Lord's service is the way of plodding perseverance in the doing of apparently small things." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-7/)

**v. 23: "Blessed is the one who does not fall away on account of Me."**

Enduring Word explains the Greek verb *skandalisthe* (translated "fall away" or "takes offence"): it "derives from the trapping of birds, and refers to the action that depresses the bait-stick and so triggers off the trap." Jesus knew the humble, non-political focus of His ministry was offensive to Jewish expectations, yet there was blessing for those who were not scandalised. Enduring Word also notes that the same word is used of Israel's response to Jesus in Romans 9:33 and 11:9—Israel was "scandalised." The warning applies even to John the Baptist. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-7/)

Gill says this was especially directed at John's disciples "who both doubted of Christ as the Messiah, and were offended at his popularity and success." The Arabic version renders it "blessed is he that doubts not of me." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/luke-7.html)

**v. 24: "After John's messengers had left, Jesus began to speak to the crowds about John: 'What did you go out into the wilderness to see? A reed swaying in the wind?'"**

Jesus waited until John's disciples had departed before praising John—"not caring to say any thing about him to the messengers, or whilst they were present, lest he should be charged with flattery." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/luke-7.html) The "reed swaying in the wind" represents a person who is inconsistent, wavering, and unstable, bending to every breeze of opinion. Jesus is saying that is *not* what John was. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-7/)

**v. 25: "Otherwise, what did you go out to see? A man dressed in fine clothes? Look, those who wear elegant clothing and live in luxury are found in palaces."**

Gill comments: John was "clothed with camels' hair, rough and undressed, and was girt with a leathern girdle; there was nothing in his person, mien, and garb, that was attractive." His food was locusts and wild honey, not the delicacies of kings' courts. The crowds did not trek into the wilderness to see a courtier but a prophet. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/luke-7.html) Enduring Word summarises: John "did not live for his own comfort or the approval of others. John was a chosen prophet of God, not a man-pleaser." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-7/)

## Areas Where Protestant Traditions Differ

**On John the Baptist's doubt (v. 19):** The sharpest traditional divide is between early Church and Reformation-era interpreters who say John sent for his disciples' sake (no personal doubt), and most modern evangelical interpreters who say John's faith genuinely wavered. The Pulpit Commentary explicitly sides with the modern view while acknowledging both. Gill (a Baptist Reformed commentator) holds the "no doubt" position strongly. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/luke-7.html) Enduring Word (Pentecostal/charismatic) sides with the "genuine doubt" view. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-7/)

**On the centurion's faith (vv. 6–9):** Reformed teachers (Ligonier, Calvin) emphasise that the centurion recognised Jesus' *supreme divine authority*—Calvin says "he who, by the mere expression of his will, restores health to men, must possess supreme authority." (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/faith-centurion) Baptist teacher Spurgeon emphasises the *compatibility of faith and humility* in the centurion. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-7/ — quoting Spurgeon) Desiring God (Baptist/Reformed) emphasises the centurion as a foreshadow of Gentile inclusion. (https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/the-centurion-faith-that-made-jesus-marvel)

**On the widow of Nain (v. 14):** Spurgeon's sermon treats the entire episode as a spiritual allegory for conversion—the spiritually dead cause grief to godly friends, Jesus alone can raise them, and He does so by speaking a word with his own authority. He explicitly says "all our Lord's miracles were intended to be parables." (https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/young-man-is-this-for-you)

**On "the Lord" in v. 13:** The Pulpit Commentary notes this rare usage reflects Luke's post-resurrection vantage point—Luke and Paul always thought of Jesus as the risen, enthroned Lord. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/luke/7.htm) This is consistent across traditions but the Pulpit draws special attention to it as a clue to Lukan authorship and theology.
